messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
In these lines, Majeed is not simply cold. The imperative “Wake up, Bibi” and his decision to take both of them to the village show urgency and a moment of responsibility. Carrying Jamila, even in a thin quilt, is a physical act of protection, and it temporarily suspends his apathy. Yet the language is still controlled and strategic: he announces, decides, and leads rather than merely comforting. Rahima is “bewildered” at his heels, suggesting he is managing them as much as saving them. The moonlight that blinds him also makes his inner motive ambiguous: we cannot fully see whether this is a genuine moral turn or another calculated response.

Ethically, the passage can appear deontological in its surface form: he acts to save the vulnerable because it is right, because he has a duty of care. But given his established cunning and apathy, it is more persuasive to read the action as teleological. He is likely responding to danger and calculating outcomes—removing them to the village, avoiding harm, preserving order, or protecting his own position. Goodwill may be present, but it is mixed with strategy. So the line shows a pragmatic, duty-like rescue whose core is probably well-calculated rather than pure good-will.

Palindromes: level, radar, kayak, madam, civic, refer, stats, tenet, rotor, racecar.

"In this brief passage, Majeed's apathy is not dominant; he acts promptly, physically carries Jamila, and leads Rahima away. Yet his speech is terse and strategic, and the image of moonlight blinding him leaves his interiority ambiguous. The same cunning remains: he takes charge, moves the women and child, and reduces disorder. Thus the line shows a moment of practical care rather than pure apathy.

Ethically, it is easier to read as teleological than purely deontological. Deontological saving would be an act done because it is right—because he owes protection to Rahima and Jamila as persons—regardless of what he gains. Teleological action is shaped by anticipated outcomes: safety, avoidance of scandal, preservation of household, or self-interest. Given Majeed's established cunning/apathy, the action looks calculated: he is responding to danger and managing consequences. The carrying of Jamila may appear as good-will, but the narrative has trained us to see it as a well-aimed move.

So: not pure goodwill; a pragmatic, possibly duty-like act with a teleological core."
